blocks.x: Most Christmas markets in this country are trying their best.
String some lights, sell some cider, call it a day.
New Jersey quietly built one that’s been running for a quarter century, gives its profits away, and has picked up the title of the state’s largest without most New Yorkers ever hearing about it.

The German Christmas Market of New Jersey, known to regulars by its German name Weihnachtsmärkt, is celebrating its 25th anniversary this year, running Friday, December 4 through Sunday, December 6 at the Sussex County Fairgrounds in Augusta.
And what started as a modest holiday gathering in 2001 has grown into the officially recognized largest annual Christmas market in the entire state of New Jersey, and it’s back again for 2026.
Why yes, it is indeed early to even start thinking about Christmaas, here’s why you should bookmark this escape now before the snow starts to fly.

Source / Sussex Skylands DMO
Twenty-five years, one very specific mission
This market was never just about selling ornaments.
It was built from the start as a nonprofit operation, and a quarter century later, that mission has only gotten bigger.

Last year alone, the market supported 64 different charities and donated $930,000 back into community causes. It now draws roughly 30,000 visitors annually, a serious number for an event that runs for a single weekend on a rural fairground about 50 miles from Manhattan.
That combination, real scale plus a genuine charitable backbone, is part of why NJ.com has ranked the market among the state’s top 10 things to do in December every year since 2013.
It’s not just the biggest holiday market in New Jersey, it stands out amongst the nation’s best and has been doing so nearly since its inception.

Source / Sussex Skylands DMO
What it actually feels like walking in

Picture rows of authentic wooden huts strung with lights, arranged along a fairground that backs up to open fields and rolling Sussex County hills. The air smells like sizzling bratwurst, warm gingerbread, and mulled gluhwein before you’ve even found the entrance.
Based on past years, expect the market’s usual lineup to return in some form, including:
Authentic wooden market huts selling handcrafted artisanal gifts, ornaments, and holiday goods
Traditional German food including bratwurst, goulash, sauerbraten, apple strudel, and linzer tarts
A full Biergarten pouring seasonal beers alongside warmed gluhwein and hot chocolate
Live choirs and festive entertainers performing throughout the weekend
A petting zoo with goats, sheep, llamas, and other farm animals
Horse-drawn wagon rides and pony rides scattered across the grounds
Special visits from St. Nicholas and Mrs. Claus for the kids
A tree lighting ceremony that anchors the weekend’s festive centerpiece

The market’s organizers note that the full 2026 entertainment schedule is still being finalized, so exact performers, showtimes, and any new additions for the 25th anniversary weekend should be confirmed through the market’s official website closer to December.

Source / Sussex Skylands DMO
A rural corner of New Jersey that’s worth the whole day
The market sits in Augusta, part of Sussex County’s Skylands region, roughly 45 miles northwest of New York City.

It’s the kind of area defined by lakes, rolling hills, and small towns that barely register on a typical New Yorker’s map, which makes stumbling onto a 30,000-person holiday market here feel like finding out your quiet neighbor secretly throws the best party on the block.
Nearby Sparta Township, built around scenic Lake Mohawk, adds small-town charm worth building a full day trip around.

And the fairgrounds themselves stay busy well into the season, hosting the Sussex County Harvest, Honey & Garlic Festival earlier in the fall and a rotating calendar of community events that makes it worth the drive.

Source / Sussex Skylands DMO
Tips for visiting the market
Because the market only runs one weekend a year, it’s worth treating like an event, not just a stop.
Here’s how to make the most of the trip:
Arrive earlier in the day, particularly on Saturday, since the market has been known to get crowded enough that browsing the huts can feel tight by afternoon
Bring cash, since several of the horse-drawn wagon rides, pony rides, and smaller vendor purchases run cash-only
Save room for food, and don’t fill up beforehand. The bratwurst and gluhwein are a large part of the draw
Check the weather and dress in real layers. This is an outdoor fairground market in early December, not a heated shopping mall
Budget extra time for parking and walking, since fairground lots can mean a longer walk in than a typical mall or downtown event
Book tickets online in November rather than waiting, since anniversary-year interest could push this toward its biggest turnout yet
Other holiday things to do nearby

Since the market only fills one weekend, it’s worth knowing what else lights up this stretch of Sussex County all season long, especially if you want to turn the trip into more than a single afternoon.

Just minutes from the fairgrounds, Skylands Stadium’s Light Show & Christmas Village turns the same town of Augusta into a mile-long, drive-through spectacle packed with more than two million lights, alongside a walk-through Christmas Village complete with Santa photos, a winter beer garden, s’mores by the fire pit, and carnival rides.
It typically runs from late November through early January, so you can overlap the two.

For anyone looking to stretch the visit into an overnight, Mountain Creek in nearby Vernon is the closest ski resort to the New York metro area, and its slopes usually open right around early December.
That means market weekend can double as the unofficial kickoff to ski season, with night skiing, tubing, and terrain parks all within reach.

Beyond the big-ticket options, several small towns across Sussex County host their own tree lighting ceremonies throughout late November and early December, including Sparta, Newton, Vernon, and Sussex Borough.
These are usually free, low-key affairs paired with Santa visits, caroling, and hot chocolate, the kind of thing worth checking into if you’re already in the area.
And if the weather cooperates, a short detour to Lake Mohawk in Sparta makes for a scenic stop, especially with the surrounding hills already dressed for winter.
The details
Sussex County Fairgrounds, 37 Plains Road, Augusta, NJ
December 4 – 6, 2026
Tickets go on sale online in November through the market’s official website
